verses.text: “Now these are the ordinances which you shall set before them.
“If you buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve six years and in the seventh he shall go out free without paying anything.
If he comes in by himself, he shall go out by himself. If he is married, then his wife shall go out with him.
If his master gives him a wife and she bears him sons or daughters, the wife and her children shall be her master’s, and he shall go out by himself.
But if the servant shall plainly say, ‘I love my master, my wife, and my children. I will not go out free;’
then his master shall bring him to God, and shall bring him to the door or to the doorpost, and his master shall bore his ear through with an awl, and he shall serve him for ever.
“If a man sells his daughter to be a female servant, she shall not go out as the male servants do.
If she doesn’t please her master, who has married her to himself, then he shall let her be redeemed. He shall have no right to sell her to a foreign people, since he has dealt deceitfully with her.
If he marries her to his son, he shall deal with her as a daughter.
If he takes another wife to himself, he shall not diminish her food, her clothing, and her marital rights.
If he doesn’t do these three things for her, she may go free without paying any money.
“One who strikes a man so that he dies shall surely be put to death,
but not if it is unintentional, but God allows it to happen: then I will appoint you a place where he shall flee.
If a man schemes and comes presumptuously on his neighbor to kill him, you shall take him from my altar, that he may die.
“Anyone who attacks his father or his mother shall be surely put to death.
“Anyone who kidnaps someone and sells him, or if he is found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.
“Anyone who curses his father or his mother shall surely be put to death.
“If men quarrel and one strikes the other with a stone, or with his fist, and he doesn’t die, but is confined to bed;

if he rises again and walks around with his staff, then he who struck him shall be cleared: only he shall pay for the loss of his time, and shall provide for his healing until he is thoroughly healed.
“If a man strikes his servant or his maid with a rod, and he dies under his hand, he shall surely be punished.
Notwithstanding, if he gets up after a day or two, he shall not be punished, for he is his property.
“If men fight and hurt a pregnant woman so that she gives birth prematurely, and yet no harm follows, he shall be surely fined as much as the woman’s husband demands and the judges allow.
But if any harm follows, then you must take life for life,
eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,
burning for burning, wound for wound, and bruise for bruise.
“If a man strikes his servant’s eye, or his maid’s eye, and destroys it, he shall let him go free for his eye’s sake.
If he strikes out his male servant’s tooth, or his female servant’s tooth, he shall let him go free for his tooth’s sake.
“If a bull gores a man or a woman to death, the bull shall surely be stoned, and its meat shall not be eaten; but the owner of the bull shall not be held responsible.

But if the bull had a habit of goring in the past, and it has been testified to its owner, and he has not kept it in, but it has killed a man or a woman, the bull shall be stoned, and its owner shall also be put to death.
If a ransom is laid on him, then he shall give for the redemption of his life whatever is laid on him.
Whether it has gored a son or has gored a daughter, according to this judgment it shall be done to him.
If the bull gores a male servant or a female servant, thirty shekels  of silver shall be given to their master, and the ox shall be stoned.
“If a man opens a pit, or if a man digs a pit and doesn’t cover it, and a bull or a donkey falls into it,
the owner of the pit shall make it good. He shall give money to its owner, and the dead animal shall be his.
“If one man’s bull injures another’s, so that it dies, then they shall sell the live bull, and divide its price; and they shall also divide the dead animal.
Or if it is known that the bull was in the habit of goring in the past, and its owner has not kept it in, he shall surely pay bull for bull, and the dead animal shall be his own.

footnotes.content: The laws are coming—not written in the sand, but to be set *before* the people like a lamp. God ordains justice lived out, not hidden in some priest's chamber.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Six years, then freedom—no debt unpayable, no bond forever. Even servitude has an end. I see in this the shape of God's mind: He means us to rest and be restored.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Marriage doesn't change the law. If he leaves, she goes with him—family stays whole. Love belongs to the servant too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here the law speaks a hard truth: the master's wife and children *belong to the master*. This verse pierces—not all binding choices are ours to break.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I love my master, my wife, my children—and I will not go free. He speaks his bonds aloud, making choice itself his confession.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ear bored through at the doorpost—a mark, a witness. He binds himself openly, and God Himself is called to hear it. In the Old Testament's shadow, I hear an echo of the Cross: one who loves and stays.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She does not go out as males do—different rules guard her. The law grants her a separate path, not casting her the same way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If he marries her to himself and she displeases him, he *cannot* sell her away. The law here turns tender—she may be redeemed. Her worth is not negotiable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If the master marries her to his son, she becomes *daughter*, not servant. A adoption of dignity—the household receives her as kin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Food, clothing, and marital rights—not luxury, but basics of dignity. The law name her due, plain and firm.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If these three things fail her, she may leave without price. The law itself opens the door. She is not property to be kept by force.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Strike a man dead, and die yourself—the cost is plain. Life weighs heavy. Even now, I know the law's reach: we reap what we sow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But *unintentional*—God allows the hand to slip. There is mercy for the accidental. A place of refuge waits. The Lord does not count what He did not will.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Presumptuously scheming, planning another's death—such a man is no refuge-seeker. Even the altar will not hide him. Malice has no sanctuary.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Strike your father or mother, and the sentence is death. The law honors father and mother in stone and blood. I have seen this command kept small and kept great—but never small.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Kidnap a man, sell him into chains—death is your due. The law protects freedom at its root. To steal a person is to steal from God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To curse father or mother brings the death sentence. The harshness cuts clear: the roots of respect go deep, or nothing stands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Quarrel, strike with stone or fist—a wound, but not death. The man is confined to bed. Now the law must distinguish: not all blows carry the same weight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He rises, walks with his staff—healing marks the end of debt. The striker pays only for lost time and the cost of care. Justice here means restoration, not excess.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Strike your servant or maid with a rod until death—punishment comes. The master's claim to ownership has its limit. The law says: even servants belong first to God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet if the servant rises after a day or two, no punishment—he is the master's property, and his recovery is itself the settlement. The law's logic here is hard: *if* recovery comes, the beating itself is cost enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Men fight, a pregnant woman is hurt and gives birth early—but no harm. A fine is paid, as the husband and judges determine. The law measures consequence carefully, not rushing to death.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if harm follows—if the woman or child dies—then life for life. Here the law shifts. When death comes, equivalence holds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eye for eye, tooth for tooth—the code known from oldest times. I used to read this as cruelty until I saw it plain: it *limits* revenge. The law says: no more than the injury demands. Measure for measure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Burning, wound, bruise—each meets its match in law. The principle holds: harm is answered with *equivalent* harm, not excess. Justice counts and measures.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Strike your servant's eye and destroy it—he goes free. The law buys back his freedom with an eye. Injury to a dependent is too grave to leave unchecked.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Knock out a tooth, and freedom is the price. Again: wound the servant, lose the servant. The law protects the dependent from lasting harm.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A bull gores a man to death—the bull dies, stoned. Its meat is forbidden. But the owner is not held, for the bull had no history of rage. Liability grows with knowledge.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if this bull *was known* to gore, and the master ignored warnings, then owner and bull both die. Here the law turns sharp: you cannot ignore danger you have been warned of. Negligence has a cost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If a ransom is laid on the owner's head to spare his life, he pays what is fixed. Redemption is possible when the ox has not yet proven itself a killer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Whether the gored one is son or daughter, the same judgment holds. The law shows no preference—a child is a child. Impartiality runs through it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If the gored one is a servant, thirty shekels are given to the master, and the ox is stoned. Thirty shekels—I notice this number shadows forward. The law values a servant's life in silver, and history will weigh that price.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Opens a pit or digs one and leaves it uncovered—negligence takes shape. If a bull or donkey falls, the owner bears the loss. The law reaches even into carelessness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The pit's owner makes good the loss—pays the neighbor and keeps the dead beast. Restitution is ordered plainly. Those who are careless pay.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One bull injures another and it dies—they sell the live bull, split the price, and divide the dead one too. When accident occurs between equals, loss is shared. Burden falls on both.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But if the bull was *known* to gore and the owner did nothing, then the full ox is paid back, and the dead animal is kept. Knowing negligence carries the full weight. The law will not excuse what you ignored.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
